A vast majority of the 10 early deployment sites were of this nature. 2. Independent fleet operators and multiple AV technologies will likely be deployed in an AMD. AV-based public mobility services can provide a rich mixture of AV fleets and corresponding service types to meet the mobility needs of the public, with each unique AV technology fleet independently managed. When deployed, these fleets will operate together within the AMD network “system of systems,” encompassing one or more AV fleet operators along with regional transit offerings and micromobility services. 3. The need for an operational management authority (OMA) within an AMD. An OMA should be established with authority to set guidelines and operating rules for the AV fleets deployed within the geographically defined district. The OMA may be an extension of existing traffic management or transit functions—or created specifically for the unique AV fleet operations—but is a necessary part of any deployment. 4. IRI complements vehicle sensing at complex multimodal junctions. IRI enhances management of the complex multimodal operating environment at roadway junctions within dense urban settings, particularly when multiple AV fleet technologies are operating together in mixed traffic. IRI, available for common use by all AV fleets and not dedicated to only one mobility technology, would allow AV fleet vehicles to “see around the corner,” providing them with additional sensing capability to maintain speed and safety through complex environments. This common-use IRI is also beneficial to orchestrate high-demand stations shared by multiple AV fleets, as is discussed in Phase III findings. 5. IRI planned, installed, and managed by the OMA is integral to safe AV fleet operations and overall roadway management. IRI deployed and managed by the OMA not only extends vehicle sensing but also enhances the management of mixed-used roadways and the safety of complex environments such as intersections. IRI implementation, when consistent with the principles defined by SAE as cooperative driving automation, could improve the manageability, safety, and performance of the entire mobility system—including AVs, human-operated vehicles, and vulnerable road users. Phase II of NLR’s research identified that safety aspects of AV fleet operation within an AMD call for a district management authority to set operational guidelines and rules for fully automated fleets within their jurisdiction, referred to as an OMA (Lott and Young 2021). Just as the proliferation of automobiles replaced horse-drawn carts and carriages in the urban centers of the world during the last century, so too is AV technology anticipated to replace human-operated vehicles in this century.
